title: Categorization with NLP
excerpt: Since launching my categorization tool Shoppy I've had some fun analyzing collected data which resulted in considerable complication of the prediction model. And now I feel the urge to write a deeper dive into its inner workings. I'm not sure how useful it would be for anyone who isn't a part of the Grocery Categorization industry, but hopefully some NLP tricks could be at least interesting to any general practitioner.
content_html:
Since launching my categorization tool Shoppy I've had some fun analyzing collected data which resulted in considerable complication of the prediction model. And now I feel the urge to write a deeper dive into its inner workings. I'm not sure how useful it would be for anyone who isn't a part of the Grocery Categorization industry, but hopefully some NLP tricks could be at least interesting to any general practitioner.

Please note that I'm by no means an NLP expert! Part of the reason for writing this kind of posts is to try and nerd-snipe someone who knows more into sharing their expertise.

Oh, and it's not a short one, this! Settle down :-)

Problem description

Just to remind everyone, what I'm trying to solve for my slowly developing shopping list app is suggesting grocery categories for products. So that it knows that "Milk" is dairy, "Apples" is produce and so on. This categorization helps with grouping and sorting, and it also looks nicer with colors and appropriate icons.

The usual approach to solving such problems is Machine Learning, and specifically — classification. That doesn't work for me though, as I couldn't come up with any means of collecting enough data myself, and hiring a consultancy is way above the budget of a tiny personal project.

So instead I'm manually crafting a clever algorithm with explicitly handled edge cases.

Lexing input

The first step is turning free-form input into something more formal and predictable: a set of lexemes. Step by step, it looks like this:

  1. Lowercase the input string
  2. Normalize it into the [NFD Unicode form][] — the one that separates accents from their characters, which lets me get rid of the former (not everyone bothers typing "crème fraîche" properly).
  3. Split the string into "words", ignoring everything else like punctuation and whitespace. In my case words are defined as alpha-numeric characters and an apostrophe (because I want things like "7'up" to be one word).
  4. For each word, get rid of apostrophes and stem them.
  5. Sort the resulting list of word stems.

This gives me a normalized, stable input key independent of basic morphological variants:

Whipping cream   |
whip cream       | => ["cream", "whip"]
Cream (whipping) |

A note on stemming. I'm using the original Porter algorithm. It's widely supported, but is also the most simplistic. I don't really care about the correctness of the result from the point of view of the English language. As long as the algorithm used to produce the data is the same as the one used for checking against it, I'm good.

Terms database

The straightforward design for a database is just a mapping from a whole key to a category: ["cream", "whip"] => "dairy". But that would require listing all likely real-world products: all sorts of apples, peppers, beans, etc. Which doesn't work for me since, as I mentioned, I don't have a firehose of data to fill it up.

But you'll notice that mostly all such product are defined by one word: an apple is an apple and is produce, regardless of the sort. So let's reify this in the form of a CSV file:

appl,produce
cream,dairy
soap,body
...

These one-word keys are called unigrams. To match a search query, we can simply look up every separate unigram from it in the database.

It works for surprisingly many cases, but it breaks on things like "apple juice", because despite having "apple" in it, it's a beverage, not produce.

This is fixed by making the order of rows in the database significant, so that juic,drink goes before appl,produce. Then, if several of the unigrams in a search query match, the earliest one wins.

This might smell to you like something prone to potentially irresolvable ordering cycles, but I actually found that I only really need two groups of significance:

# Derivations

juic,drink
milk,dairy
oil,pantry

# Raw

appl,produce
oliv,snack
oat,pantry

Things like "juice", "milk" and "oil" are usually derived from something, as in "apple juice", "oat milk" and "olive oil". Keeping those derivations above raw ingredients ensures those tings are categorized correctly.

And don't take the word "raw" too literally. There are things like "ketchup" in there! But since nobody puts "tomato ketchup" on their shopping list, it is considered "raw" in my domain.

Bigrams

The next problem is combinations of words. "Spaghetti squash" is not a pasta, but a kind of squash. And "apple sauce" is neither produce, nor a condiment, but a snack! In both of these examples no single unigram is enough to correctly identify the product. This means I need to consider two-word terms called bigrams:

# Derivations

appl sauc,snack
sauc,condiment

# Raw

spaghetti squash,produce
appl,produce
spaghetti,pantry
squash,produce

All bigrams come before unigrams, as their purpose is to serve as more specific disambiguations of conflicting unigrams. But this ordering is less significant than the groups (Derivations and Raw), so each of those gets their own set of bigrams.

At search query time, I produce bigrams as all possible combinations of two from the set of unigrams. Then they're added to unigrams as search terms:

def all_terms(unigrams):
    bigrams = [" ".join(c) for c in itertools.combinations(unigrams, 2)]
    return bigrams + unigrams

The lookup process stays exactly the same: just check all terms one by one.

By the way, I need this code to also work in the Kotlin code of my Android app, and since Kotlin doesn't have combinations in the standard library, I wrote a trivial recursive implementation by hand:

fun ngrams(items: List<String>, n: Int): List<String> =
    if (n == 1) {
        items
    } else {
        items.withIndex().flatMap { (index, item) ->
            ngrams(items.drop(index + 1), n - 1).map { "$item $it" }
        }
    }

Felt like solving a coding interview problem :-)

A few words about "pepper"… When combined with another word, it most often belongs in produce: "bell pepper", "chili pepper", "serrano pepper", etc. And since there are many of such, I want to classify the unigram "pepper" as produce to cover them all. However the single word "pepper" usually means ground black pepper, which is a spice! I tried to complicate the model at first, supporting wildcards like "* pepper". But I didn't find any other exception that would use it, so I de-complicated the model back and hard-coded a dumb `if` substituting "pepper" with "black pepper" before any lookups :-) Practicality beats purity!

Etymology woes

Human languages tend to merge words commonly used together. So something straight and forward becomes straight-forward and then just straightforward. I realized I need to care about it here after I collected examples like "redbull" and "lipbalm". Both should properly be spelled as two separate words, but people usually don't consult a dictionary before doing their groceries, so…

Funny factoid: "breadcrumbs" and "seaweed" are spelled as single words.

This can't be solved by spellchecking because my database doesn't contain original spelling: it has the bigram "bull red" and the unigram "balm", and they both are too far away from those search queries.

Instead, I started thinking about splitting words into syllables. To my everlasting surprise, nltk turned out to have several of those, from which I picked SyllableTokenizer. It is pretty simple, but it does work for "redbull" and "lipbalm" as you'd expect.

At first, I tried to switch the entire database to contain only syllables instead of full stemmed words, but it didn't work out. There are common syllables like "bar" and "can" that are also full words in their own right. So something like "barbecue sauce" would be split into ["bar", "be", "cue", ...] and will suddenly become a snack because I have a record saying that any kind of "bar" is a snack.

So instead I converged on a two-step lookup. First I split the search query into regular words and look them up as I did before. Then, if I didn't get a match, I split the words further into syllables and do a second lookup.

The syllabilization algorithm was another thing I had to port to Kotlin, because I couldn't find anything like that in the entire Java ecosystem. Drop me a note if you want that code for some reason.

Spell checking

Spell checking proved to be necessary nonetheless. Do you know if it's "fusilli" or "fussili"? Does "camamber(t?) has a "t" at the end? Or is it "haloumi" or "halloumi"? (Answers: 1) the former, 2) it does and 3) both spellings are correct.)

Unfortunately, a regular spell checker against English wouldn't work very well: all kinds of international foods and deliberately misspelled brand names kill the idea. Fortunately, I can spell check against my own database, which naturally represents the entire language that my app knows!

And the standard approach to spell checking is to employ some "edit distance" algorithm which shows how far apart is the spelling of two arbitrary words. I went with Damerau-Levenshtein (standard Levenshtein plus transpositions). I also had to come up with empirical numbers for maximum allowed distance depending on the word length. This was done completely unscientifically, and I expect to have to tweak it further. But for now it works!

Optimizations

The most astute reader might have already spotted a problem: what was a single hash-table lookup before the introduction of edit distance calculation has now turned into a linear search with each test being way more expensive than a straightforward string comparison.

So I had to to some low-hanging fruit plucking in terms of optimizations:

  • Assume people don't usually misspell the first letter of a word.
  • Don't bother comparing words that differ in length by more than the maximum allowed distance.
  • Don't bother comparing words with different n-grammness (like bigrams and unigrams).
  • If a search term matches exactly, don't bother two check the rest of them to find a closer match.

But I have to say that the main thing working in my favor here is that the data is just small!

"Separilla"?

I want to highlight two particularly weird wins made possible by the combined effect of syllabilization and spell checking.

  1. A single term "may o" works for: "mayo", "mayonnaise", "mayones" and even "mayochup". Syllabilizing these words produces "may" and some variant of "o"/"on"/"oc", which is then smoothed over by spell checking.

And I just want to state for the record that the existence of such a thing as "mayochup" made me die a little inside. Is the trouble of mixing mayo and ketchup by yourself in your kitchen so unfathomably hard that you need a brand to produce it for you? Geez…

  1. One of the previously unknown to me items in the feedback was submitted as "separilla", which turned out to be a misspelling of "sarsaparilla". So I picked out three syllables conveying the meaning: "sar", "pa" and "ril". And, thanks to spell checking, they're enough to cover both the correct spelling and a few incorrect ones.

Real data

Initially I thought of putting the collected data up on Kaggle, but since it's now heavily dependent on a custom algorithm, I'm just going to leave it as is in the Shoppy repo:

  • lib.py: all the functions
  • terms.csv: terms database (in a weird format of CSV-with-blank-lines-and-comments)
  • kinds.csv: hierarchy of defined categories (I didn't mention it, but you'll get the idea)

sentences.zh: 它受到广泛支持，但也是最简单的。

sentences.en: I don't really care about the correctness of the result from the point of view of the English language.
sentences.zh: 从英语的角度来看，我并不真正关心结果的正确性。

sentences.en: As long as the algorithm used to produce the data is the same as the one used for checking against it, I'm good.
sentences.zh: 只要用于生成数据的算法与用于检查数据的算法相同，我就可以了。

blocks.html_en: Terms database

sentences.en: Terms database
sentences.zh: 术语数据库

blocks.html_en: The straightforward design for a database is just a mapping from a whole key to a category: ["cream", "whip"] => "dairy". But that would require listing all likely real-world products: all sorts of apples, peppers, beans, etc. Which doesn't work for me since, as I mentioned, I don't have a firehose of data to fill it up.

sentences.en: The straightforward design for a database is just a mapping from a whole key to a category: ["cream", "whip"] => "dairy".
sentences.zh: 数据库的简单设计只是从整个键到类别的映射：[“cream”，“whip”] =>“dairy”。

sentences.en: But that would require listing all likely real-world products: all sorts of apples, peppers, beans, etc. Which doesn't work for me since, as I mentioned, I don't have a firehose of data to fill it up.
sentences.zh: 但这需要列出所有可能的现实世界产品：各种苹果、辣椒、豆类等。这对我不起作用，因为正如我提到的，我没有大量数据来填充它。

blocks.html_en: But you'll notice that mostly all such product are defined by one word: an apple is an apple and is produce, regardless of the sort. So let's reify this in the form of a CSV file:

sentences.en: But you'll notice that mostly all such product are defined by one word: an apple is an apple and is produce, regardless of the sort.
sentences.zh: 但您会注意到，大多数此类产品都是由一个词定义的：苹果就是苹果，是农产品，无论种类如何。

sentences.en: So let's reify this in the form of a CSV file:
sentences.zh: 那么让我们以 CSV 文件的形式具体化这一点：

blocks.html_en: These one-word keys are called unigrams. To match a search query, we can simply look up every separate unigram from it in the database.

sentences.en: These one-word keys are called unigrams.
sentences.zh: 这些单字键称为一元组。

sentences.en: To match a search query, we can simply look up every separate unigram from it in the database.
sentences.zh: 为了匹配搜索查询，我们可以简单地在数据库中查找每个单独的一元组。

blocks.html_en: It works for surprisingly many cases, but it breaks on things like "apple juice", because despite having "apple" in it, it's a beverage, not produce.

sentences.en: It works for surprisingly many cases, but it breaks on things like "apple juice", because despite having "apple" in it, it's a beverage, not produce.
sentences.zh: 令人惊讶的是，它适用于许多情况，但它会破坏“苹果汁”之类的东西，因为尽管里面有“苹果”，但它是一种饮料，而不是农产品。

blocks.html_en: This is fixed by making the order of rows in the database significant, so that juic,drink goes before appl,produce. Then, if several of the unigrams in a search query match, the earliest one wins.

sentences.en: This is fixed by making the order of rows in the database significant, so that juic,drink goes before appl,produce.
sentences.zh: 这是通过使数据库中的行顺序变得重要来解决的，以便 juic,drink 位于 appl,product 之前。

sentences.en: Then, if several of the unigrams in a search query match, the earliest one wins.
sentences.zh: 然后，如果搜索查询中的多个一元组匹配，则最早的一个获胜。

blocks.html_en: This might smell to you like something prone to potentially irresolvable ordering cycles, but I actually found that I only really need two groups of significance:

sentences.en: This might smell to you like something prone to potentially irresolvable ordering cycles, but I actually found that I only really need two groups of significance:
sentences.zh: 这对你来说可能像是容易出现潜在无法解决的排序周期的东西，但我实际上发现我只需要两组重要的内容：

blocks.html_en: Things like "juice", "milk" and "oil" are usually derived from something, as in "apple juice", "oat milk" and "olive oil". Keeping those derivations above raw ingredients ensures those tings are categorized correctly.

sentences.en: Things like "juice", "milk" and "oil" are usually derived from something, as in "apple juice", "oat milk" and "olive oil".
sentences.zh: 像“果汁”、“牛奶”和“油”这样的词通常源自某种东西，例如“苹果汁”、“燕麦奶”和“橄榄油”。

sentences.en: Keeping those derivations above raw ingredients ensures those tings are categorized correctly.
sentences.zh: 将这些衍生成分保留在原始成分之上可以确保这些成分被正确分类。

blocks.html_en: And don't take the word "raw" too literally. There are things like "ketchup" in there! But since nobody puts "tomato ketchup" on their shopping list, it is considered "raw" in my domain.

sentences.en: And don't take the word "raw" too literally.
sentences.zh: 并且不要太从字面上理解“原始”这个词。

sentences.en: There are things like "ketchup" in there!
sentences.zh: 里面有“番茄酱”之类的东西！

sentences.en: But since nobody puts "tomato ketchup" on their shopping list, it is considered "raw" in my domain.
sentences.zh: 但由于没有人将“番茄酱”列入他们的购物清单，因此在我的领域中它被认为是“生的”。

blocks.html_en: Bigrams

sentences.en: Bigrams
sentences.zh: 二元组

blocks.html_en: The next problem is combinations of words. "Spaghetti squash" is not a pasta, but a kind of squash. And "apple sauce" is neither produce, nor a condiment, but a snack! In both of these examples no single unigram is enough to correctly identify the product. This means I need to consider two-word terms called bigrams:

sentences.en: The next problem is combinations of words.
sentences.zh: 下一个问题是单词的组合。

sentences.en: "Spaghetti squash" is not a pasta, but a kind of squash.
sentences.zh: “意大利面南瓜”不是意大利面，而是南瓜的一种。

sentences.en: And "apple sauce" is neither produce, nor a condiment, but a snack!
sentences.zh: 而“苹果酱”既不是农产品，也不是调味品，而是一种零食！

sentences.en: In both of these examples no single unigram is enough to correctly identify the product.
sentences.zh: 在这两个示例中，没有一个一元足以正确识别产品。

sentences.en: This means I need to consider two-word terms called bigrams:
sentences.zh: 这意味着我需要考虑称为二元组的两个单词术语：

blocks.html_en: All bigrams come before unigrams, as their purpose is to serve as more specific disambiguations of conflicting unigrams. But this ordering is less significant than the groups (Derivations and Raw), so each of those gets their own set of bigrams.

sentences.en: All bigrams come before unigrams, as their purpose is to serve as more specific disambiguations of conflicting unigrams.
sentences.zh: 所有二元词都出现在一元词之前，因为它们的目的是更具体地消除冲突的一元词的歧义。

sentences.en: But this ordering is less significant than the groups (Derivations and Raw), so each of those gets their own set of bigrams.
sentences.zh: 但这种排序不如组（派生和原始）重要，因此每个组都有自己的一组二元组。

blocks.html_en: At search query time, I produce bigrams as all possible combinations of two from the set of unigrams. Then they're added to unigrams as search terms:

sentences.en: At search query time, I produce bigrams as all possible combinations of two from the set of unigrams.
sentences.zh: 在搜索查询时，我生成二元组作为一元组中两个的所有可能组合。

sentences.en: Then they're added to unigrams as search terms:
sentences.zh: 然后它们作为搜索词添加到一元组中：

blocks.html_en: The lookup process stays exactly the same: just check all terms one by one.

sentences.en: The lookup process stays exactly the same: just check all terms one by one.
sentences.zh: 查找过程完全相同：只需一一检查所有术语。

blocks.html_en: By the way, I need this code to also work in the Kotlin code of my Android app, and since Kotlin doesn't have combinations in the standard library, I wrote a trivial recursive implementation by hand:

sentences.en: By the way, I need this code to also work in the Kotlin code of my Android app, and since Kotlin doesn't have combinations in the standard library, I wrote a trivial recursive implementation by hand:
sentences.zh: 顺便说一句，我需要此代码也能在我的 Android 应用程序的 Kotlin 代码中工作，并且由于 Kotlin 在标准库中没有组合，因此我手动编写了一个简单的递归实现：

blocks.html_en: Felt like solving a coding interview problem :-)

sentences.en: Felt like solving a coding interview problem :-)
sentences.zh: 感觉就像解决编码面试问题:-)

blocks.html_en: A few words about "pepper"… When combined with another word, it most often belongs in produce: "bell pepper", "chili pepper", "serrano pepper", etc. And since there are many of such, I want to classify the unigram "pepper" as produce to cover them all. However the single word "pepper" usually means ground black pepper, which is a spice! I tried to complicate the model at first, supporting wildcards like "* pepper". But I didn't find any other exception that would use it, so I de-complicated the model back and hard-coded a dumb `if` substituting "pepper" with "black pepper" before any lookups :-) Practicality beats purity!

sentences.en: A few words about "pepper"…
sentences.zh: 关于“胡椒”的几句话……

sentences.en: When combined with another word, it most often belongs in produce: "bell pepper", "chili pepper", "serrano pepper", etc. And since there are many of such, I want to classify the unigram "pepper" as produce to cover them all.
sentences.zh: 当与另一个词组合时，它最常属于农产品：“甜椒”、“辣椒”、“塞拉诺辣椒”等。由于有很多这样的词，我想将一元词“胡椒”分类为农产品以涵盖所有这些。

sentences.en: However the single word "pepper" usually means ground black pepper, which is a spice!
sentences.zh: 然而，“胡椒”一词通常意味着黑胡椒粉，这是一种香料！

sentences.en: I tried to complicate the model at first, supporting wildcards like "* pepper".
sentences.zh: 我一开始尝试使模型复杂化，支持像“*胡椒”这样的通配符。

sentences.en: But I didn't find any other exception that would use it, so I de-complicated the model back and hard-coded a dumb `if` substituting "pepper" with "black pepper" before any lookups :-) Practicality beats purity!
sentences.zh: 但我没有找到任何其他可以使用它的异常，因此我对模型进行了简化，并硬编码了一个愚蠢的“if”，在任何查找之前用“黑胡椒”替换“胡椒”:-) 实用性胜过纯粹性！

blocks.html_en: Etymology woes

sentences.en: Etymology woes
sentences.zh: 词源困境

blocks.html_en: Human languages tend to merge words commonly used together. So something straight and forward becomes straight-forward and then just straightforward. I realized I need to care about it here after I collected examples like "redbull" and "lipbalm". Both should properly be spelled as two separate words, but people usually don't consult a dictionary before doing their groceries, so…

sentences.en: Human languages tend to merge words commonly used together.
sentences.zh: 人类语言倾向于将常用的单词合并在一起。

sentences.en: So something straight and forward becomes straight-forward and then just straightforward.
sentences.zh: 因此，一些直截了当的事情变得直截了当，然后就变得简单了。

sentences.en: I realized I need to care about it here after I collected examples like "redbull" and "lipbalm".
sentences.zh: 在收集了“红牛”和“润唇膏”等例子后，我意识到我需要关心它。

sentences.en: Both should properly be spelled as two separate words, but people usually don't consult a dictionary before doing their groceries, so…
sentences.zh: 两者都应该正确地拼写为两个单独的单词，但人们在购买杂货之前通常不会查阅字典，所以……

blocks.html_en: Funny factoid: "breadcrumbs" and "seaweed" are spelled as single words.

sentences.en: Funny factoid: "breadcrumbs" and "seaweed" are spelled as single words.
sentences.zh: 有趣的事实：“面包屑”和“海藻”被拼写为单个单词。

blocks.html_en: This can't be solved by spellchecking because my database doesn't contain original spelling: it has the bigram "bull red" and the unigram "balm", and they both are too far away from those search queries.

sentences.en: This can't be solved by spellchecking because my database doesn't contain original spelling: it has the bigram "bull red" and the unigram "balm", and they both are too far away from those search queries.
sentences.zh: 这无法通过拼写检查来解决，因为我的数据库不包含原始拼写：它有二元词“bull red”和一元词“balm”，而且它们都离那些搜索查询太远了。

blocks.html_en: Instead, I started thinking about splitting words into syllables. To my everlasting surprise, nltk turned out to have several of those, from which I picked SyllableTokenizer. It is pretty simple, but it does work for "redbull" and "lipbalm" as you'd expect.

sentences.en: Instead, I started thinking about splitting words into syllables.
sentences.zh: 相反，我开始考虑将单词拆分为音节。

sentences.en: To my everlasting surprise, nltk turned out to have several of those, from which I picked SyllableTokenizer.
sentences.zh: 令我永远惊讶的是，nltk 竟然有其中几个，我从中选择了 SyllableTokenizer。

sentences.en: It is pretty simple, but it does work for "redbull" and "lipbalm" as you'd expect.
sentences.zh: 它非常简单，但正如您所期望的那样，它确实适用于“redbull”和“lipbalm”。

blocks.html_en: At first, I tried to switch the entire database to contain only syllables instead of full stemmed words, but it didn't work out. There are common syllables like "bar" and "can" that are also full words in their own right. So something like "barbecue sauce" would be split into ["bar", "be", "cue", ...] and will suddenly become a snack because I have a record saying that any kind of "bar" is a snack.

sentences.en: At first, I tried to switch the entire database to contain only syllables instead of full stemmed words, but it didn't work out.
sentences.zh: 起初，我尝试将整个数据库切换为仅包含音节而不是完整的词干单词，但没有成功。

sentences.en: There are common syllables like "bar" and "can" that are also full words in their own right.
sentences.zh: 有一些常见的音节，如“bar”和“can”，它们本身也是完整的单词。

sentences.en: So something like "barbecue sauce" would be split into ["bar", "be", "cue", ...]
sentences.zh: 所以像“烧烤酱”这样的东西会被分成[“bar”，“be”，“cue”，...]

sentences.en: and will suddenly become a snack because I have a record saying that any kind of "bar" is a snack.
sentences.zh: 会突然变成零食，因为我有记录说任何一种“酒吧”都是零食。

blocks.html_en: So instead I converged on a two-step lookup. First I split the search query into regular words and look them up as I did before. Then, if I didn't get a match, I split the words further into syllables and do a second lookup.

sentences.en: So instead I converged on a two-step lookup.
sentences.zh: 因此，我转而采用两步查找。

sentences.en: First I split the search query into regular words and look them up as I did before.
sentences.zh: 首先，我将搜索查询拆分为常规单词，然后像以前一样查找它们。

sentences.en: Then, if I didn't get a match, I split the words further into syllables and do a second lookup.
sentences.zh: 然后，如果没有找到匹配项，我会将单词进一步拆分为音节并进行第二次查找。

blocks.html_en: The syllabilization algorithm was another thing I had to port to Kotlin, because I couldn't find anything like that in the entire Java ecosystem. Drop me a note if you want that code for some reason.

sentences.en: The syllabilization algorithm was another thing I had to port to Kotlin, because I couldn't find anything like that in the entire Java ecosystem.
sentences.zh: 音节化算法是我必须移植到 Kotlin 的另一件事，因为我在整个 Java 生态系统中找不到类似的东西。

sentences.en: Drop me a note if you want that code for some reason.
sentences.zh: 如果您出于某种原因需要该代码，请给我留言。

blocks.html_en: Spell checking

sentences.en: Spell checking
sentences.zh: 拼写检查

blocks.html_en: Spell checking proved to be necessary nonetheless. Do you know if it's "fusilli" or "fussili"? Does "camamber(t?) has a "t" at the end? Or is it "haloumi" or "halloumi"? (Answers: 1) the former, 2) it does and 3) both spellings are correct.)

sentences.en: Spell checking proved to be necessary nonetheless.
sentences.zh: 尽管如此，拼写检查还是有必要的。

sentences.en: Do you know if it's "fusilli" or "fussili"?
sentences.zh: 你知道它是“fusilli”还是“fussili”吗？

sentences.en: Does "camamber(t?)
sentences.zh: 是否有“cammber（t？）

sentences.en: has a "t" at the end?
sentences.zh: 末尾有“t”吗？

sentences.en: Or is it "haloumi" or "halloumi"?
sentences.zh: 或者是“haloumi”还是“haloumi”？

sentences.en: (Answers: 1) the former, 2) it does and 3) both spellings are correct.)
sentences.zh: （答案：1）前者，2）确实如此，3）两种拼写都是正确的。）

blocks.html_en: Unfortunately, a regular spell checker against English wouldn't work very well: all kinds of international foods and deliberately misspelled brand names kill the idea. Fortunately, I can spell check against my own database, which naturally represents the entire language that my app knows!

sentences.en: Unfortunately, a regular spell checker against English wouldn't work very well: all kinds of international foods and deliberately misspelled brand names kill the idea.
sentences.zh: 不幸的是，针对英语的常规拼写检查程序效果不佳：各种国际食品和故意拼写错误的品牌名称会扼杀这个想法。

sentences.en: Fortunately, I can spell check against my own database, which naturally represents the entire language that my app knows!
sentences.zh: 幸运的是，我可以对我自己的数据库进行拼写检查，这自然代表了我的应用程序知道的整个语言！

blocks.html_en: And the standard approach to spell checking is to employ some "edit distance" algorithm which shows how far apart is the spelling of two arbitrary words. I went with Damerau-Levenshtein (standard Levenshtein plus transpositions). I also had to come up with empirical numbers for maximum allowed distance depending on the word length. This was done completely unscientifically, and I expect to have to tweak it further. But for now it works!

sentences.en: And the standard approach to spell checking is to employ some "edit distance" algorithm which shows how far apart is the spelling of two arbitrary words.
sentences.zh: 拼写检查的标准方法是采用某种“编辑距离”算法，该算法显示两个任意单词的拼写相距多远。

sentences.en: I went with Damerau-Levenshtein (standard Levenshtein plus transpositions).
sentences.zh: 我选择了 Damerau-Levenshtein（标准 Levenshtein 加上换位）。

sentences.en: I also had to come up with empirical numbers for maximum allowed distance depending on the word length.
sentences.zh: 我还必须根据字长得出最大允许距离的经验数字。

sentences.en: This was done completely unscientifically, and I expect to have to tweak it further.
sentences.zh: 这是完全不科学的，我希望必须进一步调整它。

sentences.en: But for now it works!
sentences.zh: 但目前它有效！

blocks.html_en: Optimizations

sentences.en: Optimizations
sentences.zh: 优化

blocks.html_en: The most astute reader might have already spotted a problem: what was a single hash-table lookup before the introduction of edit distance calculation has now turned into a linear search with each test being way more expensive than a straightforward string comparison.

sentences.en: The most astute reader might have already spotted a problem: what was a single hash-table lookup before the introduction of edit distance calculation has now turned into a linear search with each test being way more expensive than a straightforward string comparison.
sentences.zh: 最精明的读者可能已经发现了一个问题：在引入编辑距离计算之前的单个哈希表查找现在已经变成了线性搜索，每个测试都比直接的字符串比较昂贵得多。

blocks.html_en: So I had to to some low-hanging fruit plucking in terms of optimizations:

sentences.en: So I had to to some low-hanging fruit plucking in terms of optimizations:
sentences.zh: 因此，我不得不在优化方面采取一些简单的做法：

blocks.html_en: • Assume people don't usually misspell the first letter of a word.

sentences.en: Assume people don't usually misspell the first letter of a word.
sentences.zh: 假设人们通常不会拼错单词的第一个字母。

blocks.html_en: • Don't bother comparing words that differ in length by more than the maximum allowed distance.

sentences.en: Don't bother comparing words that differ in length by more than the maximum allowed distance.
sentences.zh: 不要费心比较长度差异超过最大允许距离的单词。

blocks.html_en: • Don't bother comparing words with different n-grammness (like bigrams and unigrams).

sentences.en: Don't bother comparing words with different n-grammness (like bigrams and unigrams).
sentences.zh: 不必费心比较具有不同 n 语法性的单词（例如二元语法和一元语法）。

blocks.html_en: • If a search term matches exactly, don't bother two check the rest of them to find a closer match.

sentences.en: If a search term matches exactly, don't bother two check the rest of them to find a closer match.
sentences.zh: 如果搜索词完全匹配，则不必费心检查其余词以找到更接近的匹配项。

blocks.html_en: But I have to say that the main thing working in my favor here is that the data is just small!

sentences.en: But I have to say that the main thing working in my favor here is that the data is just small!
sentences.zh: 但我不得不说，这里对我有利的主要因素是数据很小！

blocks.html_en: "Separilla"?

sentences.en: "Separilla"?
sentences.zh: “塞帕瑞拉”？

blocks.html_en: I want to highlight two particularly weird wins made possible by the combined effect of syllabilization and spell checking.

sentences.en: I want to highlight two particularly weird wins made possible by the combined effect of syllabilization and spell checking.
sentences.zh: 我想强调两个特别奇怪的胜利，这些胜利是通过音节化和拼写检查的综合作用而实现的。

blocks.html_en: • A single term "may o" works for: "mayo", "mayonnaise", "mayones" and even "mayochup". Syllabilizing these words produces "may" and some variant of "o"/"on"/"oc", which is then smoothed over by spell checking.

sentences.en: A single term "may o" works for: "mayo", "mayonnaise", "mayones" and even "mayochup".
sentences.zh: 单个术语“may o”适用于：“mayo”、“mayonnaise”、“mayones”甚至“mayochup”。

sentences.en: Syllabilizing these words produces "may" and some variant of "o"/"on"/"oc", which is then smoothed over by spell checking.
sentences.zh: 对这些单词进行音节化会产生“may”和“o”/“on”/“oc”的某些变体，然后通过拼写检查进行平滑处理。

blocks.html_en: And I just want to state for the record that the existence of such a thing as "mayochup" made me die a little inside. Is the trouble of mixing mayo and ketchup by yourself in your kitchen so unfathomably hard that you need a brand to produce it for you? Geez…

sentences.en: And I just want to state for the record that the existence of such a thing as "mayochup" made me die a little inside.
sentences.zh: 我只是想郑重声明，“mayochup”这样的东西的存在让我有点死了。

sentences.en: Is the trouble of mixing mayo and ketchup by yourself in your kitchen so unfathomably hard that you need a brand to produce it for you?

content_html_zh:
自从启动我的分类工具 Shoppy 以来，我对收集的数据进行了一些有趣的分析，这导致了预测模型相当复杂。 现在我很想写一篇深入探讨其内部运作的文章。 我不确定它对于那些不属于杂货分类行业的人来说有多大用处，但希望一些 NLP 技巧至少能让所有全科医生感兴趣。

请注意，我绝不是 NLP 专家！ 撰写此类帖子的部分原因是试图吸引那些了解更多的人来分享他们的专业知识。

哦，这不是一个短的，这个！ 安家 ：-）

问题描述

只是提醒大家，我正在努力为我缓慢开发的购物清单应用程序解决的问题是建议产品的杂货类别。 这样它就知道“牛奶”是乳制品，“苹果”是农产品等等。 这种分类有助于分组和排序，并且通过颜色和适当的图标看起来也更好。

解决此类问题的常用方法是机器学习，特别是分类。 但这对我来说不起作用，因为我自己无法想出任何方法来收集足够的数据，而且聘请咨询公司远远超出了一个小型个人项目的预算。

因此，我手动设计了一个巧妙的算法，并明确处理了边缘情况。

词法输入

第一步是将自由形式的输入转变为更正式和可预测的东西：一组词位。 一步一步来看，它看起来像这样：

  1. 将输入字符串小写
  2. 将其规范化为 [NFD Unicode 形式][] — 将重音符号与其字符分开的形式，这让我摆脱了前者（不是每个人都愿意正确输入“crème fraîche”）。
  3. 将字符串拆分为“单词”，忽略标点符号和空格等其他所有内容。 就我而言，单词被定义为字母数字字符和撇号（因为我希望“7'up”之类的东西成为一个单词）。
  4. 对于每个单词，去掉撇号并词干。
  5. 对生成的词干列表进行排序。

这为我提供了一个独立于基本形态变体的标准化、稳定的输入键：

Whipping cream   |
whip cream       | => ["cream", "whip"]
Cream (whipping) |

关于词干的注释。 我正在使用原始的波特算法。 它受到广泛支持，但也是最简单的。 从英语的角度来看，我并不真正关心结果的正确性。 只要用于生成数据的算法与用于检查数据的算法相同，我就可以了。

术语数据库

数据库的简单设计只是从整个键到类别的映射：[“cream”，“whip”] =>“dairy”。 但这需要列出所有可能的现实世界产品：各种苹果、辣椒、豆类等。这对我不起作用，因为正如我提到的，我没有大量数据来填充它。

但您会注意到，大多数此类产品都是由一个词定义的：苹果就是苹果，是农产品，无论种类如何。 那么让我们以 CSV 文件的形式具体化这一点：

appl,produce
cream,dairy
soap,body
...

这些单字键称为一元组。 为了匹配搜索查询，我们可以简单地在数据库中查找每个单独的一元组。

令人惊讶的是，它适用于许多情况，但它会破坏“苹果汁”之类的东西，因为尽管里面有“苹果”，但它是一种饮料，而不是农产品。

这是通过使数据库中的行顺序变得重要来解决的，以便 juic,drink 位于 appl,product 之前。 然后，如果搜索查询中的多个一元组匹配，则最早的一个获胜。

这对你来说可能像是容易出现潜在无法解决的排序周期的东西，但我实际上发现我只需要两组重要的内容：

# Derivations

juic,drink
milk,dairy
oil,pantry

# Raw

appl,produce
oliv,snack
oat,pantry

像“果汁”、“牛奶”和“油”这样的词通常源自某种东西，例如“苹果汁”、“燕麦奶”和“橄榄油”。 将这些衍生成分保留在原始成分之上可以确保这些成分被正确分类。

并且不要太从字面上理解“原始”这个词。 里面有“番茄酱”之类的东西！ 但由于没有人将“番茄酱”列入他们的购物清单，因此在我的领域中它被认为是“生的”。

二元组

下一个问题是单词的组合。 “意大利面南瓜”不是意大利面，而是南瓜的一种。 而“苹果酱”既不是农产品，也不是调味品，而是一种零食！ 在这两个示例中，没有一个一元足以正确识别产品。 这意味着我需要考虑称为二元组的两个单词术语：

# Derivations

appl sauc,snack
sauc,condiment

# Raw

spaghetti squash,produce
appl,produce
spaghetti,pantry
squash,produce

所有二元词都出现在一元词之前，因为它们的目的是更具体地消除冲突的一元词的歧义。 但这种排序不如组（派生和原始）重要，因此每个组都有自己的一组二元组。

在搜索查询时，我生成二元组作为一元组中两个的所有可能组合。 然后它们作为搜索词添加到一元组中：

def all_terms(unigrams):
    bigrams = [" ".join(c) for c in itertools.combinations(unigrams, 2)]
    return bigrams + unigrams

查找过程完全相同：只需一一检查所有术语。

顺便说一句，我需要此代码也能在我的 Android 应用程序的 Kotlin 代码中工作，并且由于 Kotlin 在标准库中没有组合，因此我手动编写了一个简单的递归实现：

fun ngrams(items: List<String>, n: Int): List<String> =
    if (n == 1) {
        items
    } else {
        items.withIndex().flatMap { (index, item) ->
            ngrams(items.drop(index + 1), n - 1).map { "$item $it" }
        }
    }

感觉就像解决编码面试问题:-)

关于“胡椒”的几句话…… 当与另一个词组合时，它最常属于农产品：“甜椒”、“辣椒”、“塞拉诺辣椒”等。由于有很多这样的词，我想将一元词“胡椒”分类为农产品以涵盖所有这些。 然而，“胡椒”一词通常意味着黑胡椒粉，这是一种香料！ 我一开始尝试使模型复杂化，支持像“*胡椒”这样的通配符。 但我没有找到任何其他可以使用它的异常，因此我对模型进行了简化，并硬编码了一个愚蠢的“if”，在任何查找之前用“黑胡椒”替换“胡椒”:-) 实用性胜过纯粹性！

词源困境

人类语言倾向于将常用的单词合并在一起。 因此，一些直截了当的事情变得直截了当，然后就变得简单了。 在收集了“红牛”和“润唇膏”等例子后，我意识到我需要关心它。 两者都应该正确地拼写为两个单独的单词，但人们在购买杂货之前通常不会查阅字典，所以……

有趣的事实：“面包屑”和“海藻”被拼写为单个单词。

这无法通过拼写检查来解决，因为我的数据库不包含原始拼写：它有二元词“bull red”和一元词“balm”，而且它们都离那些搜索查询太远了。

相反，我开始考虑将单词拆分为音节。 令我永远惊讶的是，nltk 竟然有其中几个，我从中选择了 SyllableTokenizer。 它非常简单，但正如您所期望的那样，它确实适用于“redbull”和“lipbalm”。

起初，我尝试将整个数据库切换为仅包含音节而不是完整的词干单词，但没有成功。 有一些常见的音节，如“bar”和“can”，它们本身也是完整的单词。 所以像“烧烤酱”这样的东西会被分成[“bar”，“be”，“cue”，...] 会突然变成零食，因为我有记录说任何一种“酒吧”都是零食。

因此，我转而采用两步查找。 首先，我将搜索查询拆分为常规单词，然后像以前一样查找它们。 然后，如果没有找到匹配项，我会将单词进一步拆分为音节并进行第二次查找。

音节化算法是我必须移植到 Kotlin 的另一件事，因为我在整个 Java 生态系统中找不到类似的东西。 如果您出于某种原因需要该代码，请给我留言。

拼写检查

尽管如此，拼写检查还是有必要的。 你知道它是“fusilli”还是“fussili”吗？ 是否有“cammber（t？） 末尾有“t”吗？ 或者是“haloumi”还是“haloumi”？ （答案：1）前者，2）确实如此，3）两种拼写都是正确的。）

不幸的是，针对英语的常规拼写检查程序效果不佳：各种国际食品和故意拼写错误的品牌名称会扼杀这个想法。 幸运的是，我可以对我自己的数据库进行拼写检查，这自然代表了我的应用程序知道的整个语言！

拼写检查的标准方法是采用某种“编辑距离”算法，该算法显示两个任意单词的拼写相距多远。 我选择了 Damerau-Levenshtein（标准 Levenshtein 加上换位）。 我还必须根据字长得出最大允许距离的经验数字。 这是完全不科学的，我希望必须进一步调整它。 但目前它有效！

优化

最精明的读者可能已经发现了一个问题：在引入编辑距离计算之前的单个哈希表查找现在已经变成了线性搜索，每个测试都比直接的字符串比较昂贵得多。

因此，我不得不在优化方面采取一些简单的做法：

  • 假设人们通常不会拼错单词的第一个字母。
  • 不要费心比较长度差异超过最大允许距离的单词。
  • 不必费心比较具有不同 n 语法性的单词（例如二元语法和一元语法）。
  • 如果搜索词完全匹配，则不必费心检查其余词以找到更接近的匹配项。

但我不得不说，这里对我有利的主要因素是数据很小！

“塞帕瑞拉”？

我想强调两个特别奇怪的胜利，这些胜利是通过音节化和拼写检查的综合作用而实现的。

  1. 单个术语“may o”适用于：“mayo”、“mayonnaise”、“mayones”甚至“mayochup”。 对这些单词进行音节化会产生“may”和“o”/“on”/“oc”的某些变体，然后通过拼写检查进行平滑处理。

我只是想郑重声明，“mayochup”这样的东西的存在让我有点死了。 在厨房里自己混合蛋黄酱和番茄酱是否非常困难，以至于需要一个品牌来为您生产？ 天哪……

  1. 反馈中我之前未知的项目之一被提交为“separilla”，结果证明是“sarsaparilla”的拼写错误。 于是我挑出了三个表达意思的音节：“sar”、“pa”和“ril”。 而且，由于拼写检查，它们足以涵盖正确的拼写和一些不正确的拼写。

真实数据

最初我想将收集到的数据放在 Kaggle 上，但由于它现在严重依赖于自定义算法，因此我将其保留在 Shoppy 存储库中：

  • lib.py：所有函数
  • terms.csv：术语数据库（采用奇怪的 CSV 格式，带有空白行和注释）
  • types.csv：定义类别的层次结构（我没有提到，但你会明白的）
